Mesillat Yesharim 13:36: This is precisely the order of abstinence, for in this the Lord has chosen — since it is impossible for an entire nation to stand equally at one and the same level, for there are levels upon levels among the people, each according to his own understanding.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:37: Behold, at the very least, choice individuals will be found who prepare themselves with complete preparation, and through those who are prepared, even those who are not prepared will merit His love, blessed be He, and the resting of His Presence.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:38: And in this vein our Sages, of blessed memory, expounded concerning the four species of the lulav (Vayikra Rabbah 30): let these come and atone for those.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:39: And we have already found that Elijah, of blessed memory, said to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, in the incident of Ulla bar Koshev (Yerushalmi Terumot 8:4): when he answered him, "But is it not a Mishnah?" he replied to him: "Is it, then, a teaching for the pious?"
Mesillat Yesharim 13:40: But bad abstinence is like the way of the fools who, not content with refusing to take from the world what they have no necessity for, go further and deny themselves even what is necessary, and afflict their bodies with sufferings and strange practices that the Lord does not desire at all. On the contrary, the Sages said (Ta'anit 22b): a person is forbidden to torment himself. And regarding charity they said (Yerushalmi, end of Pe'ah): whoever needs to receive and does not receive is regarded as a shedder of blood. And so they said (Ta'anit 22b): "to every living soul" — the soul that I have given you, keep it alive. And they said (ibid. 11a): whoever sits in a fast is called a sinner — and they explained this to refer to one who cannot bear to afflict himself.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:41: And Hillel used to say (Proverbs 11:17): "the merciful man does good to his own soul" — referring to the morning meal, and he would wash his face and hands in honor of his Maker — how much more so is this fitting than for the portraits of kings, which are washed and polished (Vayikra Rabbah 34).
Mesillat Yesharim 13:42: Behold, then, the true general principle: whatever is not necessary for a person in the affairs of this world, it is proper for him to abstain from it; and whatever is necessary for him, for whatever reason it may be — since it is necessary for him, if he abstains from it, he is a sinner.
Mesillat Yesharim 13:43: Behold, this is a reliable principle, but the judgment of particular cases according to this principle is left only to one's own considered judgment, and a man is praised according to his own understanding, for it is impossible to enumerate all the particulars, since they are numerous, and a person's mind cannot encompass them all except one matter at a time, in its proper time.
Mesillat Yesharim 14:1:
The Components of Abstinence
The principal components of abstinence are three: there is abstinence in pleasures, abstinence in legal rulings, and abstinence in customs.
Mesillat Yesharim 14:2: Abstinence in pleasures is what we mentioned in the previous chapter — namely, not to take from the affairs of the world except what necessity compels; and this encompasses everything that is a pleasure to any of the senses, namely: in foods, in marital relations, in clothing, in outings, in what one hears, and all similar things — except on days when pleasure itself is a mitzvah.
Mesillat Yesharim 14:3: And abstinence in legal rulings is to be stringent in them always — to be concerned even for the opinion of a lone dissenting authority in a dispute, if his reasoning appears sound, even though the halachah is not decided according to him, on condition that his stringency does not turn into a leniency elsewhere.
Mesillat Yesharim 14:4: And to be stringent in cases of doubt, even where it would be possible to be lenient. And our Sages, of blessed memory, have already explained to us Ezekiel's statement (Chullin 37b): "Behold, my soul has not been defiled" — that he did not eat from an animal about whose status a sage had ruled leniently in a matter of doubt, and did not eat meat from "this cup, this cup." And behold, all this is certainly permitted by strict law, but he was stringent with himself.
Mesillat Yesharim 14:5: And I have already mentioned above that one should not learn from what was permitted to all of Israel that it is permitted to the abstinent, who must distance themselves from what is unseemly, from what resembles it, and from what resembles what resembles it. And so said Mar Ukva (ibid. 105a): In this matter I am vinegar the son of wine compared to my father — for when my father ate meat at this hour, he would not eat cheese until this time the next day, whereas I, in this meal, do not eat it, but in the next meal I do. And certainly the halachic ruling is not as his father practiced — for otherwise Mar Ukva would not have acted against it — but rather his father was stringent in his own abstinence, and therefore Mar Ukva called himself "vinegar the son of wine," since he himself was not as abstinent as his father.
Mesillat Yesharim 14:6: And abstinence in customs is solitude and separation from social society, so as to devote one's heart to service and to proper reflection upon it — on condition that one does not lean, even in this, to the opposite extreme; for they have already said, of blessed memory (Ketubot 17a): a person's mind should always be sociable with others. And so they said (Makkot 10a): a sword upon the enemies of Torah scholars who sit alone, one by one, and occupy themselves with Torah. Rather, a person should associate with the good for the time he needs for his study or his livelihood, and afterward withdraw into solitude to cleave to his God and to attain the ways of uprightness and true service.
Mesillat Yesharim 14:7: And included in this is minimizing one's speech and being careful to avoid idle talk, and not looking beyond one's own four cubits, and all similar matters, which a person accustoms himself to until they remain with him as a natural part of his movements.
Mesillat Yesharim 14:8: Now, these three components, although I have stated them to you in brief general terms, you can see that they encompass many of a person's activities; and I have already told you that the particulars can only be entrusted to considered judgment, to align them with the uprightness and truth of the general principle.
Mesillat Yesharim 15:1:
The Ways of Acquiring Abstinence
Now, the preferred way to acquire abstinence is for a person to reflect on the inferiority of the pleasures of this world and their lowliness in themselves, and the great evils that are likely to be born from them.
Mesillat Yesharim 15:2: For what inclines nature toward these pleasures, to the point that so much strength and so many stratagems are needed to separate oneself from them, is the enticement of the eyes, which are enticed by the appearance of things that seem, at first glance, good and pleasant — this is the very enticement that caused the first sin to be committed, as Scripture testifies (Genesis 3:6): "And the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, etc., and she took of its fruit and ate."
Mesillat Yesharim 15:3: But once it becomes clear to a person that this good is entirely false, imagined, and without any true permanence, and that its evil is real, or truly close to being born from it, he will certainly come to despise it and will not desire it at all. Therefore, this is the entire lesson that a person must teach his own mind: to recognize the weakness of these pleasures and their falseness, until he despises them of his own accord, and it is no longer hard in his eyes to send them away from him.
Mesillat Yesharim 15:4: Behold, the pleasure of food is the most tangible and most keenly felt — is there anything more fleeting and more perishable than it? For its duration lasts no longer than the passage through the throat; once it has passed from there and descended into the innards, its memory is lost and forgotten as though it had never been. And a person will be just as satisfied if he ate fattened geese as if he ate coarse bread, provided he ate enough of it to be satisfied. All the more so if he considers the many illnesses that can come upon him because of his eating, and at the very least the heaviness that overtakes him after eating, and the fumes that becloud his mind. Behold, in view of all this, a person should certainly not desire this thing, since its good is not really good and its evil is truly evil.
Mesillat Yesharim 15:5: And so with all the other pleasures of the world as well: if one reflects on them, he will see that even their imagined good lasts only a short time, while the evil that can be born from them is severe and long-lasting, so that it is not fitting for any person of understanding to place himself in such evil dangers for the gain of that small, fleeting good. And this is simple.
Mesillat Yesharim 15:6: And when a person accustoms himself and persists in reflecting on this truth, he will little by little go free from the prison of folly in which materiality imprisons him, and he will not be enticed at all by the enticements of false pleasures; then he will despise them and will know that he should take from the world only what is necessary, as I have written.
Mesillat Yesharim 15:7: And just as reflecting on this matter brings about the acquisition of abstinence, so too its acquisition is undermined by folly and by persistent association with nobles and men of high rank who pursue honor and multiply vanity; for upon seeing that preciousness and that grandeur, it is impossible that his own desire will not be aroused to covet them, and even if he does not let his inclination defeat him, in any case he will not escape a battle, and he will find himself in danger. In this vein Solomon said (Ecclesiastes 7:2): "It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting."
Mesillat Yesharim 15:8: And more precious than all is solitude, for just as it removes the affairs of the world from his eyes, so it removes desire for them from his heart; and King David, peace be upon him, already mentioned the praise of solitude, saying (Psalms 55:7-8): "Oh that I had wings like a dove! ... behold, then I would wander far off, I would lodge in the wilderness, Selah." And the prophets, Elijah and Elisha, we find, set apart their dwelling place in the mountains because of their solitude. And the early sages and pious ones, of blessed memory, followed in their footsteps, for they found this to be the most suitable means for acquiring the perfection of abstinence, so that the vanities of their fellows would not bring them, too, to become as befuddled as they were.
Mesillat Yesharim 15:9: And one of the things that must be guarded against in acquiring abstinence is that a person should not wish to skip and leap to the furthest extreme all at once, for this will certainly not succeed in his hand; rather, he should go about separating himself little by little — today acquiring a small measure of it, and tomorrow adding to it a bit more — until he becomes entirely accustomed to it, so that it truly becomes for him like a second nature.
Mesillat Yesharim 16:1:
An Explanation of the Trait of Purity (Taharah)
Purity is the rectification of the heart and thoughts. And we find this expression used by David, who said (Psalms 51:12): "Create in me a pure heart, O God."
Mesillat Yesharim 16:2: And its matter is that a person should leave no room for the inclination in his deeds, but rather all his deeds should be on the side of wisdom and fear of Heaven, and not on the side of sin and desire.
Mesillat Yesharim 16:3: And this applies even to bodily and material actions — that even after a person has already conducted himself with abstinence, that is, taking from the world only what is necessary, he still needs to purify his heart and his thought, so that even in that small amount which he does take, he should not intend at all any pleasure or desire, but rather his intention should be toward the good that results from that deed, on the side of wisdom and service.
Mesillat Yesharim 16:4: This is like the matter said of Rabbi Eliezer (Nedarim 20b): that he would uncover a handbreadth and cover two handbreadths, resembling one seized by a demon, so that he derived no pleasure at all, and performed that deed only for the sake of the commandment and the service. In this vein Solomon said (Proverbs 3:6): "In all your ways know Him, and He will make your paths straight."
Mesillat Yesharim 16:5: And indeed you must know that just as purity of thought is relevant to bodily deeds that are, in themselves, close to the inclination, so as to keep them distant from it and not let them belong to it, so purity of thought is likewise relevant to good deeds that are close to the Creator, blessed be His Name, so that they should not be distanced from Him and become instead the inclination's own — and this is the matter of "not for its own sake," mentioned many times in the words of our Sages, of blessed memory.
Mesillat Yesharim 16:6: However, the words of the Sages, of blessed memory, have already made it clear that there are various kinds of "not for its own sake."
Mesillat Yesharim 16:7: The worst of all is one who does not serve for the sake of service at all, but only to deceive people and to gain honor or money. And this is what they said of him (Yerushalmi Berachot 1): it would have been better for him had his afterbirth been turned over on his face; and of him the prophet said (Isaiah 64:5): "and we have all become like something impure, and all our righteousness is as a filthy garment."
Mesillat Yesharim 16:8: And there is another kind of "not for its own sake," which is serving in order to receive a reward, and of this they said (Pesachim 50b): a person should always occupy himself with Torah and mitzvot, even not for their own sake, for from doing them not for their own sake, one comes to do them for their own sake. But in any case, whoever has not yet come, from "not for its own sake," to "for its own sake," is still far from his perfection.
Mesillat Yesharim 16:9: However, what requires even more reflection and much labor from a person is the admixture of the forbidden — that is, sometimes a person goes and performs a mitzvah truly for its own sake, because this is what our Father in Heaven has decreed, yet he does not cease to mix in with it some other consideration, such as that people should praise him, or that he should receive reward for his deed. And sometimes, even if he does not truly intend for people to praise him, when his heart rejoices at the praise, he becomes more exacting — like the incident of the daughter of Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon (Avodah Zarah 18a): who used to take fine, graceful steps, and when she heard people saying, "How fine are the steps of this young woman," she immediately became more exacting still. Behold, this increase was born from the power of the praise she received.
Mesillat Yesharim 16:10: And indeed, even though such a small admixture of the forbidden is nullified in its minority, in any case, the deed containing such an admixture is not entirely pure; for just as nothing may be offered upon the lower altar except fine flour sifted through thirteen sieves, which has already become entirely purified of all dross, so it is impossible for anything to ascend as acceptable to the supernal altar as being of the complete and choicest service of God, except the choicest of deeds, pure of every kind of dross.
Mesillat Yesharim 16:11: And I do not say that whatever falls short of this will be rejected entirely, for the Holy One, blessed be He, does not withhold the reward of any creature, and pays the reward of deeds according to what they are. However, I am speaking of the perfect service that is fitting for all true lovers of the Lord — that only entirely pure service should be called by this name, in which the intention is directed solely toward the Name, blessed be He, and to nothing else. And whatever departs from this level, in proportion to how far it departs, so does the deficiency in it increase.
Mesillat Yesharim 16:12: This is what King David, peace be upon him, says (Psalms 73:25): "Whom have I in heaven, and having You, I desire nothing on earth." And he likewise said (Psalms 119:140): "Your word is very pure, and Your servant loves it." For truly, the true service must be purer even than gold and silver, as it is said concerning the Torah (Psalms 12:7): "The words of the Lord are pure words, silver refined in an earthen crucible, purified seven times."
Mesillat Yesharim 16:13: And whoever truly serves the Lord will not be satisfied with less, and will not consent to take silver mixed with dross and alloy — that is, a service mixed with improper intentions — but only the clean and pure, as is proper; and then he will be called one who performs the commandment as it should be performed, concerning which they said, of blessed memory (Shabbat 63a): whoever performs a commandment as it should be performed is never given tidings of evil. And so they said, of blessed memory (Nedarim 62a): do things for the sake of their own purpose, and speak of them for their own sake.
Mesillat Yesharim 16:14: This is what distinguishes those who serve the Lord with a whole heart. For whoever has not attached himself to Him, blessed be He, with true love, will find the refinement of this service to be a burden and a heavy load, for he will say: who can endure this? We are creatures of clay, born of woman; it is impossible to attain such refinement and purity.
Mesillat Yesharim 16:15: However, the lovers of the Lord and those who desire His service — their hearts rejoice to demonstrate the faithfulness of their love before Him, blessed be He, and to become ever more purified and refined; this is what David himself concluded, saying, "and Your servant loves it."
